entry: [[Iron Age]] kingdom of the ancient Near East, centered on the Armenian highlands between Lake Van, Lake Urmia, and Lake Sevan. Its territory extended over the modern frontiers of [[Turkey]], [[Iran]], [[Iraq]], and [[Armenia]]. Its kings left [[Cuneiform]] inscriptions in the Urartian language, a member of the Hurro-Urartian language family. The kingdom emerged in the mid-9th century BC and dominated the highlands in the 8th and 7th centuries BC. It frequently warred with Assyria and for a time became the most powerful state in the Near East. Weakened by constant conflict, it was conquered either by the [[Medes]] in the early 6th century BC or by [[Cyrus the Great]] in the middle of that century. It is noted for large fortresses and sophisticated metalwork.

[[Human settlement]] with high population density and an extensive built environment. Urban areas develop through [[Urbanization|urbanization]] and are classed as [[City|cities]], [[Town|towns]], conurbations, or [[Suburb|suburbs]]. In urbanism the term contrasts with [[Rural area|rural areas]] such as [[Village|villages]] and hamlets. The urban area is the core of a [[Metropolitan area|metropolitan area]], which also includes intervening rural land and satellite cities. In 2009 the world's urban population (3.42 billion) surpassed its rural population (3.41 billion), and by 2014 about 53 percent of the world's 7.3 billion people lived in urban areas. Between 1992 and 2015, urban areas grew from 33 million hectares to 71 million hectares, more than doubling in size.

Approach to designing buildings and the spaces between them, based on geographical location. It shapes the physical features of towns, [[City|cities]], and regional spaces while also weighing economic, social, and environmental value. Its scope ranges from a local street or public space to an entire city and surrounding areas. It connects [[Architecture]], landscape architecture, and [[Urban planning]], and draws on civil engineering, public administration, sociology, and urban economics. Its theory centers on public space such as streets, plazas, and parks. Planned cities existed in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas. In 9th-century England, many towns listed in the Burghal Hidage were laid out on a grid, including [[Southampton]] and Wallingford, to build a defensive network against Danish invaders.

Process of developing and designing plans for land use and the built environment, including the transportation, communications, and distribution networks that serve urban areas. Also called city or town planning, it guides how people live, work, and play in urban, suburban, and rural areas. Traditionally it followed a top-down approach to master planning, focused on efficiency, [[Sanitation]], and environmental protection. It is an interdisciplinary field drawing on [[Civil engineering]], [[Architecture]], [[Human geography]], and social science, and its sub-fields include [[Zoning]], economic development, and transportation planning. Projects range from new towns to the renewal of existing neighborhoods. Although many of [[Le Corbusier]]'s urban plans were never realized, his ideas profoundly influenced twentieth-century urban planning.

Indo-Aryan language spoken primarily in South Asia. It is the national language and lingua franca of [[Pakistan]] and an Eighth Schedule language in India, where it has official status in several states. Urdu and [[Hindi]] share a common vocabulary base, phonology, syntax, and grammar, and are mutually intelligible in colloquial speech. Formal Urdu draws its literary and technical vocabulary from Persian and [[Arabic]], while formal Hindi draws on [[Sanskrit]]. The language originated around [[Delhi]], where Khari Boli was spoken, and is written in a revised Perso-Arabic script. In 1837 it became an official language of the British [[East India Company]], replacing Persian across northern India. Ethnologue's 2026 estimate counts 246 million total speakers, making it the 10th-most widely spoken language.

[[Organic compound]] with the formula CO(NH₂)₂, also called carbamide. It is the simplest amide of carbamic acid and the main nitrogen-containing substance in the urine of mammals. The body forms urea in the [[Liver]] by condensing [[Ammonia]] and [[Carbon dioxide]] in the urea cycle, and it is the main way nitrogen is excreted. It is a colorless, odorless, highly water-soluble solid that is practically nontoxic and neither acidic nor alkaline in water. Widely used as a source of nitrogen in [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], it was synthesized from inorganic materials by [[Friedrich Wöhler]] in 1828, a milestone that contradicted vitalism, the doctrine that organic compounds could come only from living organisms.

Tube that carries urine from the [[Bladder|bladder]] to the external urethral opening. In placental mammals it runs from the bladder to the urethral meatus of the [[Penis|penis]] or [[Vulva|vulva]]. In males it also carries [[Semen|semen]] through the penis during [[Ejaculation|ejaculation]]. The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle that allows voluntary control over urination. The average adult male urethra is 18 to 20 centimeters (7 to 8 inches) long, while the female urethra is about 4 cm long and 6 mm in diameter.

Part of the excretory system of vertebrates, comprising the [[Kidney|kidneys]], ureters, [[Bladder|bladder]], and [[Urethra|urethra]]. Its main functions are to regulate blood volume and composition, control [[Blood pressure|blood pressure]], and regulate blood pH. It stores waste products, mainly [[Urea|urea]] and uric acid, before they are removed from the body. Each kidney contains nephrons, the functional units that [[Filtration|filter]] blood, reabsorb what the body needs, and excrete the rest as urine. The kidney receives between 12 and 30 percent of cardiac output, averaging about 20 percent. Healthy adults typically produce 1 to 2 liters of urine a day. The kidneys also contribute to red blood cell production and help synthesize [[Vitamin D|calcitriol]], the active form of vitamin D.

Release of urine from the [[Bladder|bladder]] through the [[Urethra|urethra]] in placental mammals, or through the [[Cloaca]] in other vertebrates. Also called micturition, it is the urinary system's form of [[Excretion|excretion]]. In healthy humans it is under voluntary control, though it can occur as a reflex in infants and people with neurological injury. Adult humans normally urinate up to seven times a day. In some animals urination marks territory or expresses submissiveness. It involves the central, autonomic, and somatic nervous systems. The lower urinary tract alternates between a storage phase, when urine collects in the bladder, and a voiding phase, when it is released. Brain centers that regulate it include the pontine micturition center, periaqueductal gray, and the [[Cerebral cortex|cerebral cortex]].

[[Paraphilia]] in which sexual excitement is associated with urine or urination. Also called urophilia, the term combines Greek words for 'urine' and 'lust'. Golden shower is slang for urinating on another person for sexual pleasure, while watersports is a more inclusive term. Omorashi, a fetish for having a full bladder, is sometimes considered part of it. In a 2010–11 survey, 36.52 percent of 1,580 valid responses from female kink participants reported urine play. The DSM-5 lists it under other specified paraphilic disorder, which requires recurrent, intense interest for at least six months that causes marked distress or impairment.

Branch of medicine focused on surgical and medical diseases of the urinary system and male reproductive organs. It covers the [[Kidney|kidneys]], [[Adrenal gland|adrenal glands]], ureters, bladder, urethra, [[Prostate|prostate]], and penis. Urologists treat conditions such as urinary tract infections and benign prostatic hyperplasia medically, and treat [[Prostate cancer|prostate cancer]], kidney stones, and stress incontinence surgically, using robotic, laparoscopic, and laser-assisted techniques. The urinary and reproductive tracts are closely linked, so disorders of one often affect the other. Urology is a surgical specialty, and many urologists complete fellowships lasting 12 to 36 months in subspecialties such as pediatric urology. As of 2022 there were 146 U.S. residency programs offering 356 positions.

Order of arachnids known as whip scorpions or vinegaroons. The name whip scorpion refers to their resemblance to true [[Scorpion|scorpions]] and their whiplike tail. When attacked, members discharge an offensive, vinegar-smelling liquid containing [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]]. They lack [[Venom|venom]]. All living members are classified in the family Thelyphonidae, and the name Uropygi was first used by Tamerlan Thorell in 1883. Whip scorpions range from 25 to 85 mm (1.0 to 3.3 in) in length. Fossils show that the group has existed since the [[Carboniferous]] period.

Constellation in the northern sky, also called the Great Bear. Its Latin name means 'greater bear', contrasting it with nearby [[Ursa Minor]]. It covers 1279.7 square degrees, the third-largest of the 88 modern constellations, and was among the 48 listed by [[Ptolemy]] in the 2nd century AD. Its seven main stars form the [[Big Dipper]], whose shape resembles a ladle, and the asterism is called the [[Plough]] in the United Kingdom. The pointer stars Dubhe and Merak help locate [[Polaris]], the North Star. The constellation is visible throughout the year from most of the [[Northern Hemisphere|Northern Hemisphere]] and appears circumpolar above mid-northern latitudes.

Constellation in the far northern sky, also called the Little Bear. Its Latin name means 'lesser bear', contrasting it with [[Ursa Major]], and in North America it is known as the Little Dipper. [[Polaris]], its brightest star, is a yellow-white supergiant and the brightest [[Cepheid variable|Cepheid variable]] in the night sky, and it has been the North Star since the medieval period. Kochab, an orange giant, is one of the 'guardians of the pole star.' Planets have been detected orbiting four of its stars. The constellation was one of the 48 listed by [[Ptolemy]] and contains an isolated [[Neutron star|neutron star]] called Calvera.

American author of speculative fiction, including science fiction set in her Hainish universe and [[Fantasy|fantasy]] novels set in Earthsea. Her literary career spanned nearly sixty years and produced more than twenty novels and a hundred short stories, along with poetry, [[Literary criticism|literary criticism]], translations, and children's books. *A Wizard of Earthsea* (1968) and *The Left Hand of Darkness* (1969) earned major critical and commercial success. *The Left Hand of Darkness* won both the Hugo and Nebula awards for best novel, making her the first woman to do so. Her work drew on [[Taoism|Taoist]] ideas, [[Feminism|feminism]], and the writings of [[Carl Jung]]. She received eight Hugo Awards and six Nebula Awards.

German politician and physician serving as president of the European Commission since 2019. A member of the Christian Democratic Union, she held federal cabinet posts under [[Angela Merkel|Angela Merkel]] from 2005 to 2019, and as defense minister, the first woman to hold that office. Her term has been marked by the [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID-19 pandemic]], the European Green Deal, and the [[Russo-Ukrainian war|Russo-Ukrainian war]]. On July 18, 2024, the [[European Parliament|European Parliament]] re-elected her with an absolute majority of 401 of 720 members. She was named the most powerful woman in the world by [[Forbes|Forbes]] in 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025.

*Urtica dioica*, a herbaceous perennial [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]] also called common or stinging nettle. Originally native to Europe, much of temperate Asia, and western North Africa, it is now found worldwide. Its leaves and stems carry hollow stinging hairs that inject histamine and other chemicals, causing a stinging sensation on contact. The plant has long been used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]], food, tea, and [[Textile|textile]] fiber. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] published the scientific name in *Species Plantarum* in 1753.

Country in southeastern South America, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay. It shares borders with [[Argentina|Argentina]] and [[Brazil|Brazil]], and its area of about 176,215 sq km includes a population of almost 3.5 million, nearly 2 million of whom live in the metropolitan area of its capital, [[Montevideo|Montevideo]]. Uruguay secured independence between 1811 and 1828, and its 1830 constitution established it as an independent state. Reforms in the early 20th century made it an advanced welfare state, earning it the nickname "Switzerland of the Americas." A 1973 coup ushered in a civic-military dictatorship that lasted until 1985. Uruguay was the first country to fully legalize [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]], and it is a founding member of the [[United Nations|United Nations]].

Major river in South America that forms parts of the boundaries of [[Brazil|Brazil]], [[Argentina|Argentina]], and Uruguay. It begins where the Canoas and Pelotas rivers join in the Serra do Mar in Brazil and flows about 1,838 km (1,142 mi). Its drainage basin covers 365,000 sq km (141,000 sq mi), and its main economic use is [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectric]] power, with dams at Salto Grande and Itá. Together with the [[Paraná River|Paraná River]], it forms the [[Estuary|estuary]] of the [[Río de la Plata|Río de la Plata]]. A submerged canyon, formed during the Ice Age, is visible at the Moconá Falls, which run parallel to the river rather than across it.

Ancient city of Sumer and Babylonia, today the archaeological site of Warka in [[Iraq|Iraq]]. Uruk was the type site for the Uruk period and played a leading role in the early [[Urbanization|urbanization]] of [[Sumer|Sumer]] in the mid-4th millennium BC. At its peak around 3100 BC, it may have had up to 50,000 residents, with 80,000 to 90,000 more in its environs, making it the largest urban area in the world at the time. The city was linked by canals to trade on the [[Euphrates|Euphrates]], and its Eanna District was dedicated to the goddess [[Inanna|Inanna]]. According to the Sumerian King List, Gilgamesh ruled Uruk in the 27th century BC, and he is the hero of the [[Epic of Gilgamesh|Epic of Gilgamesh]]. The city was abandoned shortly before or after the Islamic conquest of 633–638.

Retired [[Jamaica|Jamaican]] sprinter, widely regarded as the greatest sprinter of all time. He won eight Olympic gold medals, including the 100 meters and 200 meters at three consecutive Games (2008, 2012, and 2016). He is the world record holder in the 100 meters, the 200 meters, and the 4 × 100 meters relay. At the 2008 [[Beijing|Beijing]] Olympics he set world records in both the 100 meters and 200 meters. He also won two 4 × 100 meters relay gold medals. He won eleven World Championship titles from 2009 to 2015, was included in Time magazine's 100 Most Influential People of 2016, and retired after the 2017 World Championships.

Worldwide distributed discussion system organized into topic categories called newsgroups. Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis conceived it in 1979, and it was established in 1980. It developed from the Unix-to-Unix Copy (UUCP) dial-up network architecture. Users post messages, called articles, which interlinked news servers store and forward to one another. Usenet is the precursor to [[Internet|Internet]] forums and gave rise to or popularized terms such as "FAQ," "flame," "sockpuppet," and "spam." Its use as a text medium declined in the late 1990s, and it is now used mainly to share files.

Technical document that helps users operate a product, service, or application. Also called a user manual, owner's manual, or instruction manual, it is usually written by a technician, product developer, or customer service staff. Most guides pair text with images, such as screenshots of interfaces or simplified hardware diagrams. Contents typically include [[Safety|safety]] warnings, assembly and installation steps, operating and programming instructions, maintenance, troubleshooting, and warranty information. Many businesses offer free [[PDF|PDF]] copies online. Some manuals for computer equipment are supplied on CD-ROM, and instructional video is sometimes provided on [[DVD|DVD]].

Space in which interactions between humans and machines occur, allowing effective operation and control of a machine. The design goal is to make a machine easy, efficient, and enjoyable to operate. A user interface has layers, including a human-machine interface that connects input hardware such as keyboards, mice, and [[Touchscreen|touchscreens]] with output hardware such as [[Computer monitor|monitors]] and speakers. A graphical user interface combines a visual and a tactile interface, while command-line interfaces persist for precise, scriptable operations. Design considerations draw on ergonomics and [[Psychology|psychology]]. In complex systems the interface is typically computerized, and the software that controls its physical elements is part of it. Brain-computer interfaces use electrodes alone, dispensing with physical movement as an intermediary.

American singer, songwriter, dancer, and actor. He has sold over 100 million records worldwide and is one of the best-selling music artists of all time. His album *Confessions* (2004) is the best-selling album by a Black artist of the 21st century, supported by four consecutive U.S. number-one singles. His second album, *My Way* (1997), produced his first U.S. Billboard Hot 100 number-one single, "Nice & Slow." He has won eight [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] and starred in films such as *She's All That* (1999).
